rules.title: Docker API is exposed
rules.finding_message: The unencrypted Docker API (tcp 2375) listens on a non-loopback address; anyone who reaches it controls the host. Bind it to a Unix socket or loopback, or use TLS on 2376.
rules.explain: The Docker API on tcp 2375 has no password and no encryption. Anyone who reaches it can start a container that mounts the host's disk, which gives them root on the host. Scanners look for this port all the time.
rules.check: Remove the `tcp://0.0.0.0:2375` host from dockerd (the "hosts" entry in /etc/docker/daemon.json, or `-H` in a drop-in under /etc/systemd/system/docker.service.d/), then run `systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart docker`. Local tools use /var/run/docker.sock. For remote use, connect over SSH (`DOCKER_HOST=ssh://user@host`) or use TLS on 2376 with `--tlsverify`.

rules.title: Kubernetes kubelet API is exposed
rules.finding_message: The Kubernetes kubelet API (tcp 10250) listens on a non-loopback address; with anonymous auth on, anyone who reaches it can run commands in pods. Disable anonymous auth and firewall it to the control plane.
rules.explain: The kubelet runs the containers on a Kubernetes node. With anonymous access on, anyone who reaches tcp 10250 can list pods and run commands inside them, which usually leads to the whole cluster.
rules.check: In the kubelet config (often /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml) set `authentication: anonymous: enabled: false` and `authorization: mode: Webhook`, then `systemctl restart kubelet`. Firewall tcp 10250 so only the control plane reaches it. The kubelet must listen on the node's address, so this check keeps firing; suppress it for the node once it is locked down.

rules.title: etcd is exposed
rules.finding_message: etcd (tcp 2379) listens on a non-loopback address; without client certificates it gives full read and write access, including Kubernetes secrets. Require client TLS and firewall it to its peers.
rules.explain: etcd stores the whole state of a Kubernetes cluster, secrets included. Without client certificates, anyone who reaches tcp 2379 can read or change it, and so take over the cluster.
rules.check: Run etcd with `--client-cert-auth=true`, `--trusted-ca-file`, `--cert-file` and `--key-file`, and `https://` client URLs (kubeadm: /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml; standalone: /etc/etcd/etcd.conf or its unit). If only local clients use it, set `--listen-client-urls=https://127.0.0.1:2379`. Firewall tcp 2379 to the API servers and etcd peers.

rules.title: Ollama API is exposed
rules.finding_message: The Ollama API (tcp 11434) listens on a non-loopback address; it has no authentication, so anyone who reaches it can pull, delete and run models. Bind it to loopback (OLLAMA_HOST=127.0.0.1), or put an authenticating proxy in front.
rules.explain: Ollama's API has no login. Anyone who reaches tcp 11434 can run your models on your hardware, download or delete them, and fill the disk. Scanners find thousands of open Ollama servers.
rules.check: Run `systemctl edit ollama`, add `[Service]` and `Environment="OLLAMA_HOST=127.0.0.1:11434"`, then `systemctl restart ollama`. In Docker, publish it as `-p 127.0.0.1:11434:11434`. If other machines need it, put a reverse proxy with authentication in front.

rules.title: Telnet is exposed
rules.finding_message: Telnet (tcp 23) listens on a non-loopback address; it sends passwords in clear text. Disable it and use SSH.
rules.explain: Telnet sends everything, passwords included, as plain text, so anyone on the network path can read them. It also offers a login prompt that password guessers target.
rules.check: Find the program with `ss -tlnp 'sport = :23'`. Stop it: `systemctl disable --now telnet.socket` (Fedora/RHEL), or remove the telnet line from /etc/inetd.conf or /etc/xinetd.d/ and restart that service. Then remove the package (`dnf remove telnet-server`, or `apt purge` with the name `dpkg -l | grep telnetd` shows). Use SSH instead.

rules.title: rsh/rlogin/rexec is exposed
rules.expression: '512' in facts['port.tcp.exposed'] || '513' in facts['port.tcp.exposed'] || '514' in facts['port.tcp.exposed']
rules.finding_message: rexec, rlogin or rsh (tcp 512-514) listens on a non-loopback address; these trust host names and send credentials in clear text. Disable them and use SSH.
rules.explain: rsh, rlogin and rexec are 1980s remote login tools. They send passwords as plain text and can trust a client because of its host name alone, which is easy to fake.
rules.check: Find the program with `ss -tlnp 'sport >= :512 and sport <= :514'`: tcp 514 is also the usual port for syslog over TCP, which is fine to keep. Disable the r-services: `systemctl disable --now rsh.socket rlogin.socket rexec.socket` (Fedora/RHEL), or remove their lines from /etc/inetd.conf or /etc/xinetd.d/. Remove the package (`dnf remove rsh-server`, or `apt purge` with the name `dpkg -l | grep rsh` shows) and use SSH.

rules.title: VNC is exposed
rules.finding_message: VNC (tcp 5900) listens on a non-loopback address; it is often weakly authenticated and unencrypted. Bind it to loopback and tunnel it over SSH, or firewall it.
rules.explain: VNC gives the whole desktop to whoever logs in. Many setups use a short password or none, and the traffic is often unencrypted, so an open port invites guessing and snooping.
rules.check: Find the server with `ss -tlnp 'sport = :5900'`; it may be GNOME Remote Desktop, wayvnc or a QEMU console, each with its own setting. Loopback only: TigerVNC `localhost` in its config file (~/.config/tigervnc/config or ~/.vnc/config), x11vnc `-localhost`, then restart it. Connect through an SSH tunnel: `ssh -L 5900:localhost:5900 user@host`, then point the viewer at localhost:5900. Or firewall tcp 5900 to trusted hosts.

rules.title: Redis is exposed
rules.finding_message: Redis (tcp 6379) listens on a non-loopback address; by default it has no password and can be used to write files. Bind it to loopback, or firewall it and require authentication.
rules.explain: Redis has no password by default. Anyone who reaches tcp 6379 can read and delete all data, and a well-known trick (CONFIG SET dir) writes files such as SSH keys or cron jobs, giving them a shell on the host.
rules.check: In /etc/redis/redis.conf (or /etc/redis.conf; Valkey, which replaces Redis on newer Fedora: /etc/valkey/valkey.conf) set `bind 127.0.0.1 -::1` and `protected-mode yes`, then `systemctl restart redis` (Debian/Ubuntu: `redis-server`; Valkey: `valkey`). In Docker, publish it as `-p 127.0.0.1:6379:6379`. If other hosts need it, set a password (`requirepass`, or ACL users) and firewall tcp 6379 to those hosts.

rules.title: MongoDB is exposed
rules.finding_message: MongoDB (tcp 27017) listens on a non-loopback address. Bind it to loopback, or firewall it and enable authentication.
rules.explain: MongoDB without authentication lets anyone who reaches tcp 27017 read, change or delete every database. Automated scripts routinely wipe open MongoDB servers and leave a ransom note.
rules.check: In /etc/mongod.conf set `net: bindIp: 127.0.0.1` and `security: authorization: enabled` (create an admin user first), then `systemctl restart mongod`. In Docker, publish it as `-p 127.0.0.1:27017:27017`. If other hosts need it, keep authorization on, add the host's address to bindIp, and firewall tcp 27017 to those clients.

rules.title: Elasticsearch is exposed
rules.finding_message: Elasticsearch (tcp 9200) listens on a non-loopback address. Bind it to loopback, or firewall it and enable security.
rules.explain: Elasticsearch without security answers anyone who reaches tcp 9200: they can read every index, delete the data or hold it for ransom. Older versions shipped with security off.
rules.check: In /etc/elasticsearch/elasticsearch.yml set `network.host: 127.0.0.1` for a single host, or keep the address and set `xpack.security.enabled: true` with passwords (`elasticsearch-reset-password -u elastic`). Then `systemctl restart elasticsearch`, and firewall tcp 9200 to the hosts that query it.

rules.title: memcached is exposed
rules.finding_message: memcached (tcp 11211) listens on a non-loopback address; it has no authentication and can leak cached data. Bind it to loopback, or firewall it.
rules.explain: memcached has no login. Anyone who reaches tcp 11211 can read and change cached data, which often holds sessions or user records. Open memcached servers have also been used to amplify denial-of-service floods.
rules.check: Listen on loopback: on Debian/Ubuntu set `-l 127.0.0.1` in /etc/memcached.conf; on Fedora/RHEL set `OPTIONS="-l 127.0.0.1,::1"` in /etc/sysconfig/memcached. Add `-U 0` to turn off UDP. Then `systemctl restart memcached`. If other hosts need it, firewall the port to them (ufw or firewalld).

rules.title: ZooKeeper is exposed
rules.finding_message: ZooKeeper (tcp 2181) listens on a non-loopback address; by default it has no authentication. Firewall it to the cluster, and enable SASL or TLS.
rules.explain: ZooKeeper holds coordination data for Kafka, Hadoop and similar systems, and by default anyone who connects can read and change it. Changing it can break or redirect the services that depend on it.
rules.check: Firewall tcp 2181 so only the cluster members and their clients reach it. On a single host, set `clientPortAddress=127.0.0.1` in zoo.cfg. Turn on SASL authentication or TLS (`secureClientPort`) and set ACLs on the znodes, then restart ZooKeeper.

rules.title: Kafka is exposed
rules.finding_message: Kafka (tcp 9092) listens on a non-loopback address; the default listener is plaintext with no authentication. Firewall it to its clients, and enable SASL and TLS.
rules.explain: Kafka's default listener has no encryption and no login. Anyone who reaches tcp 9092 can read every message, write fake ones, or delete topics.
rules.check: In server.properties, on a single host bind to loopback (`listeners=PLAINTEXT://127.0.0.1:9092`). Otherwise move clients to a `SASL_SSL` listener with a SASL mechanism (`sasl.enabled.mechanisms`) and set `security.inter.broker.protocol` to match. Restart Kafka, and firewall tcp 9092 to the producers and consumers.

rules.title: CouchDB is exposed
rules.finding_message: CouchDB (tcp 5984) listens on a non-loopback address. Bind it to loopback, or firewall it and make sure an admin password is set.
rules.explain: CouchDB serves its data over HTTP on tcp 5984. Old versions started with no admin ("admin party"), so anyone could read and change everything, and some versions had bugs that let a visitor run code.
rules.check: In /opt/couchdb/etc/local.ini set `bind_address = 127.0.0.1` under `[chttpd]`, and make sure `[admins]` has an admin with a strong password. Run `systemctl restart couchdb`. If other hosts need it, keep the network address but firewall tcp 5984 to those hosts, and keep CouchDB up to date.

rules.title: Cassandra is exposed
rules.finding_message: Cassandra (tcp 9042) listens on a non-loopback address; its default authenticator allows everyone. Firewall it to its clients, and enable PasswordAuthenticator.
rules.explain: Cassandra's default AllowAllAuthenticator lets anyone who reaches tcp 9042 read and change every keyspace without logging in.
rules.check: In /etc/cassandra/cassandra.yaml set `authenticator: PasswordAuthenticator` and `authorizer: CassandraAuthorizer`, and restart Cassandra. Log in as cassandra/cassandra, create your own superuser, then remove the default one. Firewall tcp 9042 to the application hosts; on a single node, `rpc_address: 127.0.0.1` keeps it local.

rules.title: Consul HTTP API is exposed
rules.finding_message: The Consul HTTP API (tcp 8500) listens on a non-loopback address; without ACLs it can register services that run commands. Bind it to loopback, or enable ACLs and firewall it.
rules.explain: Consul's HTTP API on tcp 8500 registers services and health checks. Without ACLs, anyone who reaches it can add a check that runs a command on the host, so an open API is a remote shell.
rules.check: In the Consul config (/etc/consul.d/*.hcl) set `client_addr = "127.0.0.1"` and keep `enable_script_checks` off. Add an `acl` block with `enabled = true` and `default_policy = "allow"` (one setting per line), restart (`systemctl restart consul`), run `consul acl bootstrap`, and give agents and their clients (such as Nomad or Vault) their tokens. Only then change default_policy to "deny" and restart. Firewall tcp 8500 to trusted hosts.

rules.title: RabbitMQ management is exposed
rules.finding_message: The RabbitMQ management interface (tcp 15672) listens on a non-loopback address. Firewall it to administrators, and remove the default guest user.
rules.explain: The RabbitMQ management interface lets whoever logs in read and publish messages and change users. The default guest/guest account is a well-known password if it has been allowed from other hosts.
rules.check: Firewall tcp 15672 to administrators, or keep it local with `management.tcp.ip = 127.0.0.1` in /etc/rabbitmq/rabbitmq.conf and `systemctl restart rabbitmq-server`. Create your own admin (`rabbitmqctl add_user`, then `rabbitmqctl set_user_tags <name> administrator`), then `rabbitmqctl delete_user guest`.

rules.title: InfluxDB is exposed
rules.finding_message: InfluxDB (tcp 8086) listens on a non-loopback address; version 1 has no authentication by default. Bind it to loopback, or firewall it and enable authentication.
rules.explain: InfluxDB 1.x starts with no authentication, so anyone who reaches tcp 8086 can read your metrics and write or drop data. Metrics often reveal host names, users and the network layout.
rules.check: InfluxDB 1.x: in /etc/influxdb/influxdb.conf under `[http]` set `bind-address = "127.0.0.1:8086"` and `auth-enabled = true` (create an admin user first), then `systemctl restart influxdb`. InfluxDB 2.x always needs a token; set `http-bind-address = "127.0.0.1:8086"` in /etc/influxdb/config.toml if only local tools use it. If other hosts need it, firewall the port to them (ufw or firewalld).

rules.title: Microsoft SQL Server is exposed
rules.finding_message: Microsoft SQL Server (tcp 1433) listens on a non-loopback address; it is a common brute-force target. Firewall it to the hosts that need it.
rules.explain: SQL Server on tcp 1433 is one of the most scanned ports. Attackers guess the sa password and, once in, can run system commands through features such as xp_cmdshell.
rules.check: Firewall tcp 1433 to the application hosts that need it (`ufw allow from 10.0.0.5 to any port 1433`, or a firewalld rich rule). On Linux, `/opt/mssql/bin/mssql-conf set network.ipaddress 127.0.0.1` and `systemctl restart mssql-server` keep it local. Give sa a long random password, or disable it once another login has the sysadmin role.

rules.title: Oracle database listener is exposed
rules.finding_message: The Oracle database listener (tcp 1521) listens on a non-loopback address. Firewall it to the hosts that need it.
rules.explain: The Oracle listener on tcp 1521 is the door to the database. An exposed listener attracts password guessing against default accounts and attacks on unpatched listener bugs.
rules.check: Firewall tcp 1521 so only the application servers reach it. To keep it local, set `(ADDRESS = (PROTOCOL = TCP)(HOST = 127.0.0.1)(PORT = 1521))` in $ORACLE_HOME/network/admin/listener.ora. To limit clients, set `TCP.VALIDNODE_CHECKING = YES` and `TCP.INVITED_NODES` in sqlnet.ora. Either change needs `lsnrctl stop && lsnrctl start`.

rules.title: X11 is exposed
rules.finding_message: An X server (tcp 6000) listens on a non-loopback address; a client that is let in can read keystrokes and the screen. Start the X server with -nolisten tcp, and forward X over SSH.
rules.explain: An X server on tcp 6000 accepts remote programs that can draw on the screen, read every keystroke and take screenshots. With access control off, anyone on the network can do this.
rules.check: Start X without TCP: Xorg `-nolisten tcp`; GDM `DisallowTCP=true` under `[security]` in /etc/gdm/custom.conf (Debian/Ubuntu: /etc/gdm3/custom.conf); LightDM `xserver-allow-tcp=false`. Restart the display manager or log out and back in. Run remote graphical programs with `ssh -X` instead.

rules.title: rpcbind is exposed
rules.finding_message: rpcbind (tcp 111) listens on a non-loopback address; it lists RPC services and is used in reflection attacks. Disable it if no NFS v3 or NIS is served, or firewall it.
rules.explain: rpcbind tells callers which RPC services (NFS, NIS) run on the host, which helps an attacker map it. Open rpcbind has also been used to amplify denial-of-service floods.
rules.check: If the host neither serves nor mounts NFSv3 and uses no NIS, run `systemctl disable --now rpcbind.service rpcbind.socket` (NFSv3 mounts need it, through rpc-statd; an NFSv4-only server needs `vers3=n` under `[nfsd]` in /etc/nfs.conf, then `systemctl mask rpcbind.service rpcbind.socket rpc-statd.service`). Otherwise firewall tcp and udp 111 to the NFS hosts.

rules.title: NFS is exposed
rules.finding_message: NFS (tcp 2049) listens on a non-loopback address. Export only to the hosts that need it, and firewall it.
rules.explain: NFS shares files over the network and trusts the client's own word about which user it is. Anyone who reaches tcp 2049 from an address an export allows can read or write those files, often as any user.
rules.check: In /etc/exports, list only the hosts or subnet that need each share, e.g. `/srv/share 192.168.1.0/24(rw,root_squash)`, never `*`, then run `exportfs -ra`. Firewall tcp 2049 to the same hosts. If the host should not serve files, run `systemctl disable --now nfs-server`.

rules.title: TFTP is exposed
rules.finding_message: TFTP (udp 69) listens on a non-loopback address; it has no authentication. Disable it, or firewall it to the boot network.
rules.explain: TFTP hands out and accepts files with no login at all. Anyone who reaches udp 69 can download what it serves, often network-boot images or device configs with passwords, and may upload files if writing is allowed.
rules.check: If the host does not serve network boot, stop it: `systemctl disable --now tftp.socket` (Fedora/RHEL) or `systemctl disable --now tftpd-hpa` (Debian/Ubuntu), and remove the package. If it does, bind it to the boot network (tftpd-hpa: `TFTP_ADDRESS="192.168.1.1:69"` in /etc/default/tftpd-hpa), keep it read-only, and firewall udp 69 to that network. dnsmasq can also serve TFTP (`enable-tftp`).

rules.title: FTP is exposed
rules.finding_message: FTP (tcp 21) listens on a non-loopback address; it sends passwords in clear text. Use SFTP, or firewall it.
rules.explain: FTP sends user names, passwords and files as plain text, so anyone on the network path can read them. FTP servers are also a common target for password guessing.
rules.check: Use SFTP, which comes with SSH (`sftp user@host`), then `systemctl disable --now vsftpd` (or proftpd) and remove the package. If FTP must stay, in vsftpd.conf (/etc/vsftpd.conf or /etc/vsftpd/vsftpd.conf) set `ssl_enable=YES` with `rsa_cert_file` and `rsa_private_key_file` pointing at a certificate and key, `force_local_logins_ssl=YES` and `anonymous_enable=NO`, restart it, and firewall tcp 21.

rules.title: SMB is exposed
rules.finding_message: SMB (tcp 139 or 445) listens on a non-loopback address. Firewall it to the networks that need file sharing.
rules.explain: SMB is Windows-style file sharing. Exposed SMB is a top target for password guessing and has had bugs that let worms spread on their own (WannaCry). It should never be reachable from the internet.
rules.check: With Samba, under `[global]` in /etc/samba/smb.conf set `interfaces = lo 192.168.1.0/24` and `bind interfaces only = yes` (or `hosts allow = 192.168.1.`), then `systemctl restart smb` (Debian/Ubuntu: `smbd`). Firewall tcp 139 and 445 to the LAN. If no shares are needed, `systemctl disable --now smb nmb` (Debian/Ubuntu: `smbd nmbd`).

rules.title: SNMP is exposed
rules.finding_message: SNMP (udp 161) listens on a non-loopback address; v1/v2c community strings are sent in clear text. Firewall it, or use SNMPv3.
rules.explain: SNMP v1 and v2c use a "community string" as the password and send it as plain text; the default "public" is often left in place. Anyone who reaches udp 161 can then read the host's processes, network and software, and sometimes change settings.
rules.check: In /etc/snmp/snmpd.conf listen locally or on the management network only (`agentaddress udp:127.0.0.1:161`), remove `rocommunity`/`rwcommunity` lines and `com2sec ... public` lines (Fedora's default), and use an SNMPv3 user with authentication and encryption (`net-snmp-create-v3-user -ro -a SHA -x AES <name>` while snmpd is stopped; on Debian/Ubuntu it is in libsnmp-dev). Run `systemctl restart snmpd`, and firewall udp 161 to the monitoring server.

rules.title: PostgreSQL is exposed
rules.finding_message: PostgreSQL (tcp 5432) listens on a non-loopback address. Bind it to loopback, or firewall it to the hosts that need it.
rules.explain: A database open to the network is open to password guessing, and one weak or reused password gives away all the data. PostgreSQL superusers can also run programs on the host.
rules.check: In postgresql.conf (Debian/Ubuntu: /etc/postgresql/<version>/main/; Fedora/RHEL: /var/lib/pgsql/data/) set `listen_addresses = 'localhost'`, then `systemctl restart postgresql`. In Docker, publish it as `-p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432`. If other hosts need it, allow only them in pg_hba.conf with `scram-sha-256`, and firewall tcp 5432 to them.

rules.title: MySQL is exposed
rules.finding_message: MySQL or MariaDB (tcp 3306) listens on a non-loopback address. Bind it to loopback, or firewall it to the hosts that need it.
rules.explain: A database open to the network is open to password guessing, and one weak account can give away all the data. MySQL and MariaDB servers are scanned constantly.
rules.check: Set `bind-address = 127.0.0.1` under `[mysqld]` (Debian/Ubuntu: /etc/mysql/mariadb.conf.d/50-server.cnf or /etc/mysql/mysql.conf.d/mysqld.cnf; Fedora/RHEL: a file in /etc/my.cnf.d/), then `systemctl restart mariadb` (or `mysql`, `mysqld`). In Docker, publish it as `-p 127.0.0.1:3306:3306`. If other hosts need it, limit their accounts to their address ('app'@'10.0.0.5') and firewall tcp 3306 to them.

rules.title: Cleartext LDAP is exposed
rules.finding_message: LDAP (tcp 389) listens on a non-loopback address; binds without StartTLS send passwords in clear text. Require StartTLS or use LDAPS on 636, and firewall it.
rules.explain: LDAP often holds every user and group, and simple logins (binds) without StartTLS send passwords as plain text. Anonymous binds can also hand the whole directory to anyone who connects.
rules.check: With OpenLDAP, first give slapd a certificate (`olcTLSCertificateFile` and `olcTLSCertificateKeyFile` on cn=config, both in one ldapmodify) and test `ldapsearch -ZZ -x -H ldap://<host>`. Then require TLS for password binds with `olcSecurity: simple_bind=128` (not `tls=1`, which also refuses ldapi and every client without TLS), and refuse anonymous binds with `olcDisallows: bind_anon`. Firewall tcp 389 and 636 to the hosts that use the directory.

rules.title: Kibana is exposed
rules.finding_message: Kibana (tcp 5601) listens on a non-loopback address. Bind it to loopback, or firewall it and enable security.
rules.explain: Kibana shows everything stored in Elasticsearch. Without security, anyone who reaches tcp 5601 can read the logs and data, and older versions had bugs that let a visitor run code on the server.
rules.check: In /etc/kibana/kibana.yml set `server.host: "127.0.0.1"` and reach it through a reverse proxy or an SSH tunnel, then `systemctl restart kibana`. If others must reach it directly, turn on Elasticsearch security (`xpack.security.enabled: true`) so Kibana asks for a login, and firewall tcp 5601.

rules.title: RDP is exposed
rules.finding_message: RDP (tcp 3389) listens on a non-loopback address; it is a common brute-force target. Firewall it, require Network Level Authentication, or reach it through a VPN.
rules.explain: RDP is one of the most attacked ports on the internet: password guessing, and bugs such as BlueKeep that need no login. Ransomware groups often get in this way.
rules.check: On Linux this is usually xrdp or GNOME Remote Desktop. Firewall tcp 3389 to the LAN or a VPN (`ufw allow from 192.168.1.0/24 to any port 3389`, or a firewalld zone with that source). For xrdp you can also keep it local with `port=tcp://127.0.0.1:3389` in /etc/xrdp/xrdp.ini, `systemctl restart xrdp`, and an SSH tunnel. Use strong passwords; on Windows require Network Level Authentication.

rules.title: WinRM over HTTP is exposed
rules.finding_message: WinRM over HTTP (tcp 5985) listens on a non-loopback address. Firewall it to administrators, or use HTTPS on 5986.
rules.explain: WinRM gives remote command-line control of Windows. Over plain HTTP on tcp 5985 it is a common target for password guessing and for moving from one taken machine to the next.
rules.check: On Windows, allow it only from admin hosts (`Set-NetFirewallRule -Name WINRM-HTTP-In-TCP -RemoteAddress 192.168.1.10`), or move to HTTPS on 5986 (`winrm quickconfig -transport:https`, with a certificate) and delete the HTTP listener. On Linux, `ss -tlnp 'sport = :5985'` shows which program listens (for example OMI) so you can stop or firewall it.

rules.title: SSH is exposed
rules.finding_message: SSH (tcp 22) listens on a non-loopback address. If the host is reachable from untrusted networks, allow keys only and firewall it.
rules.explain: SSH open to the internet gets password guessing all day. With keys and no passwords that is just noise, but one weak password lets an attacker in as that user.
rules.check: Keep your session open. Install your key (`ssh-copy-id user@host`) and test a key login in a second session. Then set `PasswordAuthentication no` and `PermitRootLogin prohibit-password` in /etc/ssh/sshd_config, and in any /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ file that sets them (the first value read wins, e.g. 50-cloud-init.conf). Run `sshd -t`, then `systemctl reload sshd` (Debian/Ubuntu: `ssh`). Before a firewall goes on, allow your own address first, then limit the rest, or use a VPN. On a LAN-only host, suppress this finding.

rules.title: Prometheus node_exporter is exposed
rules.finding_message: Prometheus node_exporter (tcp 9100) listens on a non-loopback address; it shows host details to anyone who reaches it. Firewall it to the Prometheus server.
rules.explain: node_exporter publishes detailed host metrics: services, disks, network interfaces and software versions. That is a map for an attacker, and anyone who reaches tcp 9100 can read it without a login.
rules.check: Firewall tcp 9100 so only the Prometheus server reaches it (`ufw allow from <prometheus-ip> to any port 9100`, or a firewalld rich rule). If Prometheus runs on the same host, start node_exporter with `--web.listen-address=127.0.0.1:9100` (Debian/Ubuntu: ARGS in /etc/default/prometheus-node-exporter) and restart it. It also supports TLS and a password via `--web.config.file`.

rules.title: Telnet server is installed
rules.expression: 'inetutils-telnetd' in facts['package.names'] || 'telnet-server' in facts['package.names'] || 'telnetd' in facts['package.names']
rules.finding_message: A telnet server package is installed. Remove it and use SSH.
rules.explain: A telnet server lets people log in over a connection that sends passwords as plain text. Even when it is not running, an installed server can be switched on by mistake later.
rules.check: Remove it: `dnf remove telnet-server` (Fedora/RHEL) or `apt purge <name>` (Debian/Ubuntu) with the name `dpkg -l | grep telnetd` shows (telnetd or inetutils-telnetd). Use SSH for remote logins.

rules.title: rsh server is installed
rules.finding_message: An rsh server package is installed. Remove it and use SSH.
rules.explain: rsh, rlogin and rexec send passwords as plain text and can trust a client by host name alone, which is easy to fake. With the server installed, it can be switched on by mistake later.
rules.check: Remove it: `dnf remove rsh-server` (Fedora/RHEL) or `apt purge <name>` (Debian/Ubuntu) with the name `dpkg -l | grep rsh` shows (rsh-server or rsh-redone-server). Use SSH for remote logins.

rules.title: NIS server is installed
rules.finding_message: A NIS server package (ypserv or nis) is installed; NIS sends password hashes to any client that asks. Remove it and use LDAP or local accounts.
rules.explain: NIS shares user accounts across hosts, but it hands out password hashes to any client that asks, so anyone on the network can collect them and crack them offline.
rules.check: Move the accounts to LDAP (for example FreeIPA or OpenLDAP) or to local accounts first, then remove it: `dnf remove ypserv` (Fedora/RHEL) or `apt purge nis` (Debian/Ubuntu; this also removes the NIS client).

rules.title: TFTP server is installed
rules.expression: 'atftpd' in facts['package.names'] || 'tftp-server' in facts['package.names'] || 'tftpd' in facts['package.names'] || 'tftpd-hpa' in facts['package.names']
rules.finding_message: A TFTP server package is installed; TFTP has no authentication. Remove it unless the host serves network boot.
rules.explain: TFTP serves and accepts files with no login. If the server runs, anyone on the network can fetch the files it holds, such as boot images or device configs that contain passwords.
rules.check: If the host does not serve network boot, remove it: `dnf remove tftp-server` (Fedora/RHEL) or `apt purge <name>` (Debian/Ubuntu) with the name `dpkg -l | grep tftpd` shows. If it does, keep it, firewall udp 69 to the boot network, and suppress this finding for the host.

rules.title: xinetd is installed
rules.finding_message: The xinetd package is installed; it is mostly used to run legacy cleartext services. Remove it and run what is needed as systemd services.
rules.explain: xinetd starts network services on demand. Today it is mostly used for old cleartext services such as telnet, rsh or tftp, and it hides them from the usual systemd tools.
rules.check: See what it runs: `grep -l 'disable *= *no' /etc/xinetd.d/*`. Move anything still needed to a systemd service or socket, then remove it: `dnf remove xinetd` (Fedora/RHEL) or `apt purge xinetd` (Debian/Ubuntu).

rules.title: talk server is installed
rules.expression: 'inetutils-talkd' in facts['package.names'] || 'talk-server' in facts['package.names'] || 'talkd' in facts['package.names']
rules.finding_message: A talk server package is installed; talk is an unencrypted legacy service. Remove it.
rules.explain: talk is an old chat service between users. It sends everything unencrypted, has a history of security bugs, and nothing current needs it.
rules.check: Remove it: `dnf remove talk-server` (Fedora/RHEL) or `apt purge <name>` (Debian/Ubuntu) with the name `dpkg -l | grep talkd` shows (talkd or inetutils-talkd).

rules.title: OpenVIBES test program is running
rules.finding_message: The OpenVIBES test program (openvibes-test finding) is running; findings work on this host. Stop it with Ctrl-C.
rules.explain: This is not a security problem. It is a pipeline test that fires on purpose while the openvibes-test program runs, to prove that this host's findings reach the console.
rules.check: Nothing to fix. Stop the test program with Ctrl-C, or let it finish.
